<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.17</span> The Levi-Civita theorem (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/levi-civita-connection.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Levi_Civita_Connection">7.3</a>)</h1></header>
<p>Let <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, g)\)</span> be a metric manifold. We show that <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> is well defined on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>, and that any torsion-free, metric-compatible connection <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span>. That <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> is torsion free and metric compatible was shown in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Metric">7</a>. In a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>, let <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{ji}\)</span> be the connection coefficient functions of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Torsion freeness.</em> <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^m_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ji} - \Gamma^m_{ij} = 0\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^m_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ji}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Metric compatibility.</em> By (<a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/levi-civita-connection.html#eq_metric_compatibility" data-kind="equation" data-label="eq_metric_compatibility">7.3</a>), <span class="math inline">\((\nabla_{\partial x_k} g)_{ij} = 0\)</span> reads  <span class="math display">\[
            \partial_k g_{ij} = \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} + \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im} .
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p><em>Cyclic permutations.</em> Writing the last relation for the cyclic permutations <span class="math inline">\((k, i, j)\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\((i, j, k)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((j, k, i)\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \partial_k g_{ij} &amp;= \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj} + \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im}, \\
            \partial_i g_{jk} &amp;= \Gamma^m_{ji} \, g_{mk} + \Gamma^m_{ki} \, g_{jm}, \\
            \partial_j g_{ki} &amp;= \Gamma^m_{kj} \, g_{mi} + \Gamma^m_{ij} \, g_{km},
        \end{align*}</span>  adding the last two and subtracting the first,  <span class="math display">\[
            \partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ki} - \partial_k g_{ij}
            = \Gamma^m_{ji} \, g_{mk} + \Gamma^m_{ij} \, g_{km}
            + \underbrace{\Gamma^m_{ki} \, g_{jm} - \Gamma^m_{ik} \, g_{mj}}_{= \, 0}
            + \underbrace{\Gamma^m_{kj} \, g_{mi} - \Gamma^m_{jk} \, g_{im}}_{= \, 0}
            = 2 \, g_{km} \, \Gamma^m_{ij},
        \]</span>  where the underbraced terms cancel, and the remaining two coincide, by the symmetry of <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span> in its lower indices and of <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Solving for <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span>.</em> Multiplying by <span class="math inline">\(\frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{lk}\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\((g^{-1})^{lk} \, g_{km} = \delta^l_m\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\[
            \Gamma^l_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} (g^{-1})^{lk} \big( \partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ki} - \partial_k g_{ij} \big)
            = \big( \Gamma^{\text{LC}}_\mathscr{X} \big)^l_{ij} .
        \]</span>  The connection coefficient functions are the Christoffel symbols in every chart, so <span class="math inline">\(\nabla = \nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Well-definedness.</em> In each chart domain <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>, the Christoffel symbols define, through the component formulas of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>, a connection on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>, torsion free and metric compatible. On <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\)</span>, the connections of both charts are torsion free and metric compatible, so by the previous items they coincide: the Christoffel symbols of the two charts obey the transformation law of connection coefficient functions, and assemble into a single connection <span class="math inline">\(\nabla^{\text{LC}}\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>. <span class="math inline">\(\square\)</span></p></li>
</ul>
